issues.issue: The identity of the "Buyer" — its name, state of organization and address — and the date of the Agreement are left blank, so the instrument does not on its face show who is bound or when. A court would have to construe whether the assignee developer or GSA is the "Buyer" and whether a binding contract was formed at all.

The "Property" is fixed by Exhibit A's legal description and "approximately 10.89 acres," but Section 3 requires a deed containing "new legal descriptions" reflecting the vacation of Sixth and Abbott Streets and the contiguous properties thereby created. Whether the vacated street parcels are part of the "Property" sold cannot be settled from this clause alone.

This clause conveys Seller's interest in adjoining street beds only "to the center line thereof," while Section 3 contemplates conveyance of the whole contiguous parcels created by vacating Sixth Street and Abbott Street. The two cannot both fix the extent of the street-bed interest conveyed.

"All proper instruments" for conveyance and for "the assignment and collection of any such award" is undefined and unbounded, and the obligation is open-ended in time ("or thereafter, on demand"). A court would have to decide what documents Seller can be compelled to sign and for how long.

The "total purchase price" is stated as a fixed $9,000,000, yet the same section makes $1,000,000 of it payable only out of TIF reimbursements and reducible by setoffs. Whether $9,000,000 is a firm price or a ceiling is not resolvable from this sentence read with the rest of Section 2.

"Standard deductions and prorations" and "customary closing expenses" set no ascertainable measure of what may be added to or subtracted from the $8,000,000 due at Closing. The parenthetical's list (utility and real estate tax prorations) may or may not exhaust "customary" expenses.

"Less any deductions identified below" points to deductions that are nowhere identified below in this Agreement; the only deduction machinery (the $500,000 Due Care Limitation of Liability) sits in the Option, not here. The cross-reference has no referent in its own instrument.

Payment of the balance "at a rate of 10% of the annual tax incremental financing reimbursement received by Buyer" makes the last $1,000,000 contingent on TIF receipts, which cannot be squared with Section 8(a)(i)'s requirement that Buyer pay "the Purchase Price" at Closing. Whether Seller has an unconditional debt or only a share of TIF proceeds turns on which provision controls.

The clause is cast as an illustration ("For example... anticipated... an estimated $200,000") yet defines the operative term "Outstanding Balance," and it makes the balance reducible by "setoffs as described below" when no setoffs are described below in this Agreement. Both the binding force of the example and the source of the setoffs are open.

Interest accrues only "to the same extent, if any" that Detroit or Michigan pays interest to Buyer on "outstanding incurred eligible expenses," a measure that is neither defined nor tied to the Outstanding Balance's amount or period. The rate, base and timing of Seller's interest are indeterminate.

This sentence is duplicated verbatim in Section 28 except that Section 28 says "less any setoff" where this says "less any deductions." A court would have to decide whether "deductions" and "setoff" describe the same reductions to the Outstanding Balance.

"Permitted Exceptions" is defined here by reference to items identified in an undated Real Estate Option Agreement, while Section 4 speaks of "those Permitted Exceptions attached hereto" and the attachment list names an Exhibit B — Permitted Exceptions. The two definitions of the same defined term cannot both govern.

The Title Company's office location is left blank, and Section 8(a) makes "the office of the Title Company" the place of Closing. The clause therefore fails to fix the very location the closing provision depends on.

"Shall have ten (10) business days prior to the date of Closing" does not say when the cure period begins or whether it is a ten-day window ending at Closing, leaving Seller's cure deadline indeterminate. The phrase can be read as a deadline, a duration, or a condition on Closing.

This clause refers to "those Permitted Exceptions attached hereto," but Section 3 defines Permitted Exceptions as the items identified in the Real Estate Option Agreement rather than any attachment. Which set of exceptions is "permitted" cannot be answered without reconciling the two.

Buyer must elect "prior to the expiration of the period for Seller to remedy" the exceptions, yet the election is triggered only "If Seller is unable" to remedy them — an event not knowable until that period expires. The sequencing of trigger and deadline is internally impossible.

The Title Company is to issue "an owner's title insurance policy or title commitment therefore," leaving it unsettled whether Buyer receives a policy or merely a commitment at closing. "In the amount of the Purchase. Price" also invokes a capitalized term Section 2 never formally defines.

The survey obligation has no delivery deadline at all — it is conditioned only on execution by both parties — and it is further conditioned on the City's "final approved plat of vacation," an approval this Agreement does not require anyone to obtain. When, if ever, the survey is due is indeterminate.

Buyer's acceptance of the Property with all environmental conditions cannot easily be squared with Section 7(d) and 7(e), in which Seller expressly represents the Property's environmental condition and its compliance with hazardous-substance laws. Whether the acknowledgment waives those representations is the question.

The carve-out "except as expressly set forth elsewhere in the Agreement" appears only in this sentence and not in the surrounding as-is language, so its reach over the rest of Section 6 is unclear. What "expressly set forth elsewhere" captures is itself undefined.

Buyer's agreement to take the Property with all faults "whether now or hereafter existing" contradicts Section 11, which places the risk of loss on Seller until delivery of the deed and requires Seller to repair injury beyond ordinary wear and tear. Both cannot govern damage occurring between signing and closing.

The representations mix a knowledge qualifier ("no knowledge of any reason," "to its knowledge") with what reads as an unqualified assurance that "possession of the land has been peaceable and undisturbed." Which assurances are knowledge-limited and which absolute is not clear from the words used.

This utility representation is limited to availability "for its current use" and omits gas, whereas Section 26 repeats the identical representation without the current-use limitation and includes gas. The scope of the utility assurance differs between the two provisions.

Seller represents it has provided "all environmental information that it has," a standard tied to Seller's own undefined holdings and not to any objective completeness. What information Seller "has" — including reports held by agents or consultants — is left open.

The representations are qualified "Except as otherwise indicated on Schedule A attached," but no Schedule A is attached to this Agreement — the attachment list names only Exhibit A and Exhibit B, and Schedule A is an attachment to the Option. The exceptions to Seller's environmental representations therefore have no identified content in this instrument.

Representations that "will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter" have no end point, while Section 23 fixes survival as running only until fulfillment and GSA's written acceptance of occupancy. The duration of Seller's warranty obligations depends on which sentence controls.

The outside closing date runs "ninety (90) days after the execution of this Agreement," while Section 9 of the Option fixes Closing at no later than 90 days after exercise of the Option, and the execution date in this Agreement's preamble is blank. The controlling closing deadline cannot be fixed from this clause alone.

This subsection requires Buyer to pay "the Purchase Price" at Closing, but Section 2 makes only $8,000,000 payable at Closing and defers the remaining $1,000,000 to future TIF receipts. The two provisions state different closing obligations for the same payment.

The deed is to be subject to the Permitted Exceptions "and any exceptions created or suffered by Buyer," a carve-out absent from Section 3, which requires title free of all liens subject only to Permitted Exceptions. The permitted state of title at closing differs between the two provisions.

The subsection is numbered (iv) but its final sentence limits "This Section 8(a)(v)," which is the possession clause, so the extraordinary-obligations proviso attaches to the wrong subsection on its face. A court would have to decide which subsection the limitation qualifies.

The clause requires delivery of "the Title Policy" as a capitalized term, but Section 4 defines only "Title Commitment" and "Title Company" and allows issuance of either a policy or a commitment at closing. What must be delivered into escrow is therefore uncertain.

Splitting "the charges of the Title Company for such closing" 50/50 sits uneasily with Section 4, which puts the title commitment and policy at "Sellers sole cost and expanse." Which Title Company charges are shared and which are Seller's alone is unresolved.

"All real estate taxes, expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use of the Property" is an open-ended category with no enumeration or limit, unlike Section 2's narrower "utility and real estate tax prorations." What expenses are prorable is left to argument.
The post-closing true-up runs from when information "is available," with no outside date and no standard for when availability occurs or who must pursue it. The obligation has no ascertainable end.

The ninety-day window for a specific performance suit runs from "the date of Seller's failure or refusal to comply," which may precede the written notice and the five-day cure period that define default. When the limitation period starts is ambiguous on the face of the sentence.

"Liquidated damages not to exceed $50,000, either a $50,000 letter of credit or cash equivalent" is internally inconsistent as to amount, and the security is required both "upon the execution of this Agreement" and "within ten (10) business days of Award and Assignment of the Option," two different times, with "Award" nowhere defined. The amount and timing of Buyer's security cannot be fixed from the words used.

Designating the $50,000 as liquidated damages cannot be squared with the closing sentence of Section 10 permitting the parties to "seek any other remedy available at law or in equity." Whether Seller's recovery is capped at $50,000 depends on which sentence controls.

This clause presupposes that GSA may revoke "the Assignment to the Buyer," but Section 13 of the Option makes the Option freely assignable and provides no mechanism or ground for revocation of an assignment. The condition on which Buyer recovers its security has no counterpart in the governing instrument.

"Any subsequent Buyer" is undefined and this Agreement contains no assignment provision creating one, yet the clause requires such a person to post security "upon the execution of this Agreement," an event a subsequent buyer would not participate in. Who must post and when is indeterminate.

Preserving "any other remedy available at law or in equity" cannot be squared with the preceding sentences of Section 10, which confine Buyer to specific performance or actual damages and cap Seller's recovery at $50,000 in liquidated damages. Whether the enumerated remedies are exclusive is squarely in doubt.

Placing risk of loss on Seller until delivery of the deed conflicts with Section 6, in which Buyer accepts the Property in its condition at closing with all faults "whether now or hereafter existing." Both cannot govern loss occurring between signing and closing.

"Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear" and "an appropriate deduction from the purchase price" supply no measure of either the triggering damage or the price adjustment, and the choice between repair and deduction is unallocated. Neither party's entitlement on a casualty is ascertainable.

"Substantial portion" is defined circularly as a portion that "would impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Real Property" — "affect" has no threshold and "Real Property" is not the defined term "Property." Whether a given taking triggers the termination right turns on undefined words.

The ten-day period runs from Buyer's "receipt... of written notification of any such condemnation," but the clause does not say who must give that notification or make Seller's notice a condition of waiver. Whether the right to terminate can be waived absent notice from Seller is open.

"Insubstantial" is defined by the same circular test — a portion that "would not impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Property" — with no threshold for "affect," so a taking could satisfy neither definition or arguably both. The line between the substantial and insubstantial branches is unascertainable.

The inspection right is granted "during the period of this Option including any extension periods," but this instrument is a purchase and sale agreement with no Option period of its own, and under Section 2 of the Option that period ends on exercise. When Buyer's entry right begins and ends has no referent in this Agreement.

The clause imposes duties on "Optionee" and rights on "Optionor," terms this Agreement never defines — its parties are "Seller" and "Buyer." Who must require the insurance and whose acceptance measures it is unstated in this instrument's own vocabulary.

"Said parties" has no clear antecedent in a provision that has just referred to representatives, agents and "offerors participating in the lease procurement process," and the clause imposes no obligation on Buyer itself for its invitees' damage. Who bears the restoration duty is uncertain.

The notice duty is placed on "Optionee" and owed to "Optionor," neither of which is a defined party to this Agreement, and "reasonable notice" fixes no period. The obligation cannot be applied to Buyer and Seller without construction.

The address block for notices "If to Buyer" is left blank, so no notice can be validly addressed to Buyer under the clause's own terms. The "With copy to" GSA line also appears under the Seller heading, leaving unclear whose notices must be copied to the Government.

The deemed-receipt rule supplies dates only for mail and overnight courier, omitting personal delivery, which the preceding sentence expressly authorizes as method (ii). When a personally delivered notice is effective is left unstated.

The representation is that no commission is payable "to any other person or entity for brokerage or similar services performed hereunder," which is limited to services under this Agreement and says nothing about brokers engaged in connection with the Option or the underlying transaction. The scope of "performed hereunder" is arguable.

Making time of the essence "throughout the term of this Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 8(a), which fixes Closing only on "a mutually agreeable date," and with the blank execution date from which the ninety-day outside date runs. Which dates are strict cannot be settled from this clause alone.

"Legal holiday" is not defined, and this transaction involves a Michigan property, an Illinois-based federal agency and a federal Buyer's assignee, so federal and state holiday calendars may differ. Which calendar extends a performance date is unspecified.

Choosing the law of the state where the Property is located cannot be squared with Section 19 of the Option, which subjects the transaction to the Contract Disputes Act and federal dispute resolution, the Buyer being GSA's assignee. Whether Michigan law or federal law governs disputes is contestable.

The Agreement binds "permitted assigns" although it contains no assignment provision defining what an assignment is or how consent is given. What makes an assign "permitted" is unstated in this instrument.

A prevailing-party fee-shifting clause is difficult to square with Section 19 of the Option, which channels disputes into the Contract Disputes Act against the United States, where such fees are not ordinarily recoverable by contract. Whether the clause is enforceable in that forum is open.

This clause requires amendments to be "in writing and executed by each party hereto," while Section 24 requires execution by the Buyer, Seller and the Government acting by GSA. The two amendment formalities cannot both be satisfied by the same instrument.

Survival runs "until fulfilled, up to and including the time of completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy of such improvements" by GSA — events this Agreement neither requires nor schedules, and which may never occur. The end of the survival period is indeterminate.

The clause says this Agreement "cancels and supersedes all prior agreements" while in the same breath preserving the August 2006 Real Estate Option Agreement — itself a prior agreement — as one of the only two agreements between the parties. Whether the Option survives this Agreement, and which controls in conflict, cannot be told from the words used.

Section 18 of the Option names the Option, Exhibit 1 and the recorded Memorandum of Option as the only agreements, while this clause names only this Agreement and the Option. Whether the Memorandum remains in force is left unresolved between the two integration clauses.

Disclaiming all representations "other than those expressly contained herein" is in tension with the preceding sentence, which makes the Option part of the parties' embodied agreement and preserves its representations. Whether Seller's Option representations survive the disclaimer is the question.

Amendment is conditioned on execution by "the Government, acting by GSA," which is not a signatory to this Agreement — the signature blocks provide only for Seller and Buyer. Whether a non-party's signature can be a condition of amendment, and whose it must be if the Option has been assigned, requires construction.

The bar on recording this Agreement or "any memorandum or short form hereof" sits against the Memorandum of Real Estate Option Agreement, Exhibit 3 to the Option, which was executed expressly for recording to give notice of the right to purchase. Whether that recorded memorandum offends this prohibition is arguable.

This utility statement adds gas and drops the "for its current use" qualifier that limits the identical representation in Section 7(c). Whether the utilities are warranted adequate for the contemplated federal facility or only for current use turns on which version governs.

Making utility terminations and relocations "the sole responsibility of Buyer" cannot be squared with Section 12 of the Option, under which Optionor is responsible at its own expense for the governmental approvals covering street vacations and utility relocation. Who bears relocation cost and effort is unresolved between the instruments.

Seller's duty is only to "cooperate" in securing Brownfield Plan approval, while Section 12 of the Option obliges Optionor affirmatively to draft the Brownfield Plan, submit it, and obtain approval by a fixed date. Whether Seller owes a duty of result or only of cooperation depends on which controls.

This sentence duplicates the closing sentence of Section 2 but conditions the Buyer's entitlement on repayment of the Outstanding Balance "less any setoff" rather than "less any deductions." Whether "setoff" and "deductions" mean the same reductions, and which text governs, is left to construction.
